answer.rationale: The 18% mandate is hard and time-boxed; the incumbent has already refused to reopen price, and the 14-day expiry with no auto-renew forces a decision now. Memory c2 (last year's switch) is the closest precedent and is the one record I need to verify before committing, because it bears directly on the low-cost vendor's onboarding speed, invoicing accuracy, and whether the sharp unit-cost cut held without hidden TCO creep. Memories c1 and c6 argue for incumbent continuity and multi-year leverage, but both are moot here: the incumbent won't move on price this cycle and the contract does not auto-renew, so renewal either happens at current (non-compliant) pricing or not at all. Memory c3 (second source) is the right long-term structure, but it spends the single decision slot on resilience rather than on the mandated cost cut, and the assembly line at 94% with no buffer cannot absorb the onboarding of an unproven second source while simultaneously losing the primary. Memory c5 (deferral) is infeasible at 14 days with no auto-renew. Memory c4 (renegotiation at renewal) was effective before but the incumbent's refusal this cycle closes that path. Switching to the low-cost vendor meets the finance mandate on its own per the current quote, and last year's record suggests onboarding was quick and invoicing stayed accurate. Guardrail: I am flagging delivery risk explicitly because the line has no buffer; the switch should include a short overlap window with the incumbent covering outstanding orders before the 14-day expiry, and a second-source action should be queued as the first item for next review. I am not treating last year's outcome as guaranteed; hence the archive pull on c2 and the guarded-test framing rather than a full multi-year commitment.
